meta.title: Retrieval — did the right memory reach the prompt
meta.description: Whether the ledger's recall puts the right memory in the prompt: recall@k, MRR and latency for the policies that exist today — random, recency and tag match plus recency — against an oracle ceiling, over a seeded synthetic corpus at two sizes.
meta.liveSkipped: --live not requested (and not applicable: no ranked policy exists yet)
meta.note: The corpus is synthetic: statements composed from twenty topic vocabularies, with distractors built to defeat one cheap signal each — the same tag with a different fact, and the same words with a different fact. These numbers measure whether a retrieval POLICY can find the right record among distractors, which is a mechanism; they say nothing about whether any model understands language, and no row here involves one.

headline.title: Tag match and recency, scored — the number a ranker would have to beat
headline.text: Over 10,000 memories and 160 questions, today's recall — tag match, then recency — puts a gold memory in the top 10 for 1.3% of questions and in first place for 0.6% (MRR 0.007). Recency alone manages 0.0% and a seeded random draw 0.0%, against an analytic floor of 0.1%; the oracle row is 1.000 everywhere, which is what proves the scorer. At 1,000 memories the same policy reaches 17.5% — the drop to 10,000 is the size at which the question becomes hard, and the reason the number is published at both. 40 of the 160 questions never name a tag, and for those the incumbent IS recency. No ranker exists yet; when one does, its row goes beside these, whichever way it falls. The corpus is synthetic — statements composed from 20 topic vocabularies, with same-tag and same-words distractors — so read every row as a mechanism: whether a policy can find the right record among distractors, not whether a model understands language.
